sections.title: Pollution: air, water and land
sections.body: Pollution means harmful substances being released into the environment, where they damage living things and their habitats. There are three main types. Air pollution comes mainly from burning fossil fuels — vehicle exhaust and smoke from factories and power stations — as well as haze and construction dust. Water pollution comes from chemical waste and oil spills, sewage, fertilisers washed off farms, and plastic rubbish. Land pollution comes from rubbish and hazardous waste left on the ground. Pollutants harm living things in many ways: tiny particles in the air irritate the windpipe and air sacs and cause breathing problems; chemicals in a river can poison fish directly or use up the dissolved oxygen so the fish suffocate; and poisons can build up along a food chain, becoming most concentrated in the top predators.
sections.terms: pollution, air pollution, water pollution, land pollution, pollutants, dissolved oxygen

sections.title: The greenhouse effect and global warming
sections.body: Some gases in the air, called greenhouse gases, trap heat from the Sun like a blanket around the Earth. Carbon dioxide is the most important one. A natural amount keeps the Earth warm enough for life, but humans add extra carbon dioxide — mostly by burning fossil fuels in vehicles, factories and power stations, and by cutting down and burning forests. More greenhouse gas traps more heat, so the Earth slowly warms; this is global warming. Its effects are serious: polar ice melts and sea levels rise, flooding low-lying coasts; weather becomes more extreme; and warmer conditions even let mosquitoes breed and spread disease faster. This is why switching off lights, using less electricity and planting trees all help — they cut the carbon dioxide we add to the air.
sections.terms: greenhouse gas, carbon dioxide, global warming, fossil fuels, climate change

sections.title: Deforestation and habitat loss
sections.body: Deforestation is the clearing of large areas of forest for farmland, cities or wood, and it harms the environment in several linked ways. With fewer trees, less carbon dioxide is removed from the air and less oxygen is produced, which worsens global warming. Fewer trees also mean less transpiration, so less water vapour enters the air — reducing cloud formation and rainfall in that region. Tree roots normally hold the soil together; without them, rain washes the soil away, causing soil erosion. Most importantly, forests — especially tropical rainforests — are home to a huge variety of living things, so clearing them destroys habitats and threatens countless species.
sections.terms: deforestation, habitat, transpiration, soil erosion, rainforest, biodiversity

sections.title: Protecting living things and biodiversity
sections.body: Biodiversity is the great variety of living things in an ecosystem. Every species has a role — in food chains, in pollinating plants, or in dispersing seeds — so losing even one can affect many others, and once a species is extinct it is gone forever. That is why people protect endangered animals such as tigers and pandas, and special habitats such as coral reefs and mangroves, which shelter thousands of sea species and protect coastlines from waves. Bees and birds matter too, because they pollinate many of our food crops. Countries also set rules limiting how many fish may be caught, so that enough breeding fish are left for populations to recover instead of collapsing from overfishing.
sections.terms: biodiversity, ecosystem, extinction, endangered species, coral reef, overfishing

sections.title: Conserving resources: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
sections.body: Many of Earth's resources are limited, so we should not waste them. The three R's help cut down waste. Reduce means using less in the first place, such as switching off lights you do not need. Reuse means using the same item again — for example carrying a refillable water bottle instead of buying new plastic ones; reusing is the best choice because no energy is needed to remake the item. Recycle means turning old materials into new ones: recycling paper saves trees, and recycling metal cans uses only a small fraction of the energy needed to make new metal. Saving water and electricity matters too — take shorter showers, fix leaks, use LED bulbs and a fan instead of air-conditioning. Plastic is a special problem because it does not break down for hundreds of years and harms wildlife, so reducing plastic use is very important.
sections.terms: reduce, reuse, recycle, conserve, plastic, resources

sections.title: Greener choices and Singapore's efforts
sections.body: Everyday choices add up. Travelling by bicycle, or by shared public transport like the MRT, uses far less fuel per person than driving, so less carbon dioxide and pollution are released. Electric cars produce no exhaust gases at all. Eating less meat helps too, because producing meat uses a lot of land and water and releases methane, a greenhouse gas. Singapore, being small with limited land and water, makes special efforts: it plants many trees to absorb carbon dioxide, cool the city and shelter wildlife; it collects rainwater in reservoirs, recycles used water into NEWater, and saves water carefully; and it builds vertical farms and uses more solar power to produce food and clean energy locally. Each of these choices reduces our impact on the environment.
sections.terms: public transport, electric car, methane, NEWater, solar power, conservation

sections.title: What is an adaptation?
sections.body: An adaptation is a special feature of a living thing — either a body part (structural) or a behaviour (something the organism does) — that helps it survive and reproduce in its habitat. Plants and animals that fit well to their environment can find food, avoid predators, keep their body conditions stable, and pass on their adaptations to their young. Living things in very different places (polar regions, deserts, rainforests, the ocean) have developed very different adaptations because each habitat poses different challenges. When the environment changes faster than living things can adapt — for example, when a habitat is destroyed or the climate shifts — many species struggle to survive.
sections.terms: adaptation, structural, behavioural, habitat, survive, reproduce

sections.title: Structural and behavioural adaptations
sections.body: Structural adaptations are about an organism's body — the shape, parts, or covering it is born with. Body coverings like fur, feathers, scales, or thick skin keep the body at the right temperature. Mouthparts are shaped for what an animal eats: sharp teeth for tearing meat, flat teeth for grinding plants, long beaks for sipping nectar, or sharp beaks for cracking seeds. Body colour and patterns help with camouflage, communication or warning. Behavioural adaptations are the things an organism does. Animals that migrate move to where conditions are better when seasons change. Some hibernate through the cold months, using stored fat for energy. Other behaviours include hunting in groups, building shelters, caring for young, or burrowing during the hot part of the day. Many living things rely on both structural and behavioural adaptations together to survive.
sections.terms: structural adaptation, behavioural adaptation, camouflage, migration, hibernation

sections.title: Cold-climate adaptations
sections.body: Animals that live near the poles must keep heat from escaping their bodies and find food when the surroundings are frozen. The polar bear is a classic example. Its thick fur traps a layer of air, and air is a poor conductor of heat — so heat from its body cannot escape easily. Underneath the fur, a thick layer of fat called blubber gives more insulation and stores energy. The fur is white, helping the bear camouflage against the snow and ice as it stalks seals. Its ears are small and rounded — less surface area means less heat is lost to the cold air. Wide paws spread the bear's weight on snow and act like paddles when it swims. Penguins use a similar set of tricks: feathers that overlap tightly to trap warm air, blubber underneath, and huddling together as a behaviour to share warmth and protect chicks from the wind.
sections.terms: polar bear, thick fur, blubber, insulator, camouflage, small ears

sections.title: Desert plant adaptations
sections.body: A desert is hot during the day, cold at night, and gets very little rain. Plants there must reduce the water they lose and store as much as they can collect. The cactus is a model desert plant. Its leaves have been reduced to sharp spines, which means the plant has a much smaller surface area for water to escape from — and the spines also stop thirsty animals from eating the plant. A thick, fleshy stem with a waxy coating stores water from the rare rains and reduces evaporation. Cactus roots are wide but shallow, so they can soak up surface water quickly whenever it does rain. Some desert plants stay as seeds in the soil for years, only sprouting after a heavy rainfall — that way the young plants grow when there is enough water to survive.
sections.terms: spines, waxy coating, water storage, shallow roots, evaporation

sections.title: Desert animal adaptations
sections.body: Desert animals also have to deal with high temperatures and little water. The camel — sometimes called the 'ship of the desert' — has several adaptations that work together. Its humps store fat (not water, as is commonly thought); the camel breaks down this fat for energy and to make water inside its body when food is scarce. Long eyelashes and slit-like nostrils keep blowing sand out. Big, wide feet stop it from sinking into soft sand. A camel can drink huge amounts of water at once and lose a large fraction of its body water before becoming unwell — most other mammals cannot. Many smaller desert animals (lizards, foxes, scorpions) use behavioural adaptations instead, burrowing during the hot day and coming out at night when it is cool.
sections.terms: hump, fat storage, long eyelashes, wide feet, nocturnal, burrow

sections.title: Avoiding predators: camouflage, mimicry and warning colours
sections.body: Living things have many ways to avoid being eaten. Camouflage makes the animal hard to see against its surroundings — a green grasshopper on a leaf, or a brown moth on tree bark — so predators do not spot it. Some animals use mimicry: a moth wing with large eye-spots looks like the face of a bigger animal, scaring or confusing predators that might attack. Brightly coloured frogs, snakes and insects often have a different trick called warning colouration — predators learn that the bright colours mean a bad taste or a poison and avoid those animals. Hard sharp spines (like on a hedgehog or sea urchin), shells (like on a tortoise or snail), and tough skin all give physical protection. Some sea creatures are nearly transparent so predators look right through them, and large numbers of fish swim in shoals so any one fish has a smaller chance of being caught.
sections.terms: camouflage, mimicry, warning colouration, spines, shoal
